items.title: Jamey Aebersold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 26, 2022
items.q: So when it came to saxophone players I heard Charlie Parker well I don’t know what to think about him.

ctx.x: I think it’s also Ted Nash.

Yes, right. I think the one I listened to was his uncle or granddad. But anyhow I listened to him a lot and I had a quartet record from the Westlake School of Music out in California with a tenor, piano, bass and drums. And I don’t know whatever happened to them but I played that over and over. I had an Oscar Peterson — excuse me — Oscar Pettiford record that I bought, and then I bought — my first LP — my first 78 was Duke Ellington on two sides. “Tootin’ Through the Roof” was one of the tunes and I forget what…

Wayne Shorter and Michael Brecker, etcetera, etcetera. But in the early stages I listened to all those people. And I also listened to trios, piano trios, bass players. I’ve probably got twelve, thirteen thousand LPs, maybe more than that.

items.title: Aebersold Jamey — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: they got me listening to Charlie Parker and different people.

ctx.x: But there was never any kind of challenge or animosity?

I don’t think so. Not that I remember. Maybe it went right over my head because I was so involved in the music. When I was in high school, though... I was 15 years old. The bass player with this Fairlane Ford, he had heard about some lessons in jazz over in Louisville. I think it was 10 bucks probably for 10 lessons. He kept asking me, and I kept saying, “No,” because I was just nervous. But finally I relented, and we went over, and I remember standing there with my saxophone, and there were these guys who I…
people. Because they were Louisville beboppers at the time, making a living.
